title: Unity guide pilot
introduction: Bahá’u’lláh asks why God created everyone from the same dust, and answers at once: so that no one should exalt himself over another. The rabbis of the Mishnah had asked the same question of Adam and given the same answer, and from that meeting point this pilot lets other voices sit beside the first hundred quotations of the guide. Some stand close: Saʿdī and Paul on the body whose members suffer together, Confucius on reciprocity, a Zulu proverb on what makes a person, King on the single garment of destiny. Others push back, or add what is missing. Aristotle warns that a city made perfectly one is no longer a city; the story of Babel has God scatter a united people; Gandhi wants every culture to blow through his house and refuses to be blown off his feet; Du Bois asks to keep two names where ‘Abdu’l-Bahá hopes for one. The Bahá’í passages are not softened by the company, and the other voices are not made to agree with them. Each is placed beside the reading it answers, with a note saying why.
questions: What do the images of dust, tree, body, sea and lamp each claim about human oneness? What do Saʿdī, Paul, the hadith and Marcus Aurelius add to the image of the body, and where do their settings or scope differ from the Bahá’í passages?

The readings hope for one city, one nation and one common Faith. Set beside them Aristotle on the unity that destroys a city, the scattering at Babel, Micah’s vine and fig tree, and Qur’an 5:48. What distinguishes the unity the readings intend from uniformity?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá says religion must cause love, and that if it causes enmity its absence is preferable. How do Swift, Pascal, Penn and Gandhi each respond to the same failure? What would count as evidence that a religion unites?

The circle of unity widens from family to continent. Compare the Great Learning, Burke’s “little platoon”, Mozi and Mencius. Does a wider loyalty depend on a nearer one, compete with it, or change it?

Which practices in these readings challenge racial prejudice? Read the garden of many colours beside the melting pot and the orchestra, and “close your eyes to racial differences” beside Harlan and Blackmun. What does each image ask of a community?

Emerson, Gibran, Gandhi and Du Bois each defend something that unity might cost: the self, the space between two people, a place to stand, a second name. Which of their concerns do the Bahá’í passages already answer, and which remain open?

findings.title: The cut is not a summary of the guide.
findings.text: Taking the first hundred quotations keeps the opening of the guide and loses the rest of its argument: conduct, consultation and the Covenant, institutions, peace and prayer do not appear, and nothing here answers to them.

findings.title: Outside voices gather where the imagery is.
findings.text: Readings built on an image or an argument (dust, body, tree, lamp, garden, the widening circle) drew several parallels each. Readings that restate a principle or address the Bahá’í community drew few or none, so the outside quotations are not spread evenly.

findings.title: A parallel is rarely an equivalent.
findings.text: Most of the quotations placed “alongside” share an idea with their reading and differ in scope: a congregation, the believers, one nation. The notes say so in each case; without them the page would suggest agreements that are not there.

findings.title: “Cultural currency” has a centre of gravity.
findings.text: Chosen for their currency in English, forty of the hundred come from modern Europe and North America and thirteen from the King James Bible. Asia, Africa and the Islamic world are present in smaller numbers, and each of their voices needed a translation whose wording and rights had to be settled first.

findings.title: Popular is not the same as checkable.
findings.text: Several of the most widely shared sayings on unity have no traceable source, and the best-known modern ones are in copyright or are song lyrics. The hundred here are those whose wording could be copied from a page and checked against it.

outside.why: The rabbis ask the reading’s own question, why humankind began from a single person, and give its answer: so that no one can claim a greater ancestor than another. The Mishnah says it in a courtroom, while warning witnesses in a capital case.

The reading asks people made of one substance to walk with the same feet and eat with the same mouth. A Roman emperor uses the same parts of one body and reaches the same duty from nature alone: to work against one another is unnatural.

A father teaches his son with the reading’s image of many waters and one sea. His point is that creatures do not know they come from the one True; the reading names the one Being and leaves the forgetting unsaid.

Kabīr’s hymn, kept in the Sikh scripture and using a Muslim name for God, joins the two opening readings: if the whole universe welled up from one Light, on what ground is one person ranked above another?

“Regard ye not one another as strangers,” says the reading. The Torah makes the same demand a law, for a people who remember being strangers themselves, and gives the measure: love the stranger as yourself.
A line from a Roman comedy, spoken by a man defending his interest in a neighbour’s troubles, became the classical motto for the reading’s thought that no human being is a stranger to another.

The reading calls unity a spiritual sword, and a later one says the Prophets came to unite and not to disperse. In the Gospel the sword is the division a new message brings into a household. Must a call to unity divide before it unites?

The reading likens existence to a human body whose finest nerves must help one another. Saʿdī said it of humankind six centuries earlier and added a test: whoever feels nothing at another’s pain does not deserve the name of human.

Paul’s body, whose members cannot dismiss one another and suffer together, is the nearest scriptural parallel to the reading. He is writing to one congregation about its quarrels; the reading speaks of the whole world of existence.

The same body with the same symptom: when one part ails, the whole lies awake in fever. The saying describes the community of believers; beside the reading it raises the question of how far the body extends.

Letters mean nothing singly, says the reading, but joined in words they have an effect that was hidden before. Aristotle states the general point in the language of philosophy: a true whole is something more than a heap of its parts.

The reading grounds brotherhood in one God, one humankind, one globe and one sky. Speaking of a rival power in the Cold War, an American president keeps the globe and the air, adds children and mortality, and makes no appeal to religion.
Schiller’s brotherhood arrives through joy, which mends what custom has divided. The reading reaches the same word by counting its grounds one by one, from a common Creator to a shared sea and tree.

The reading sets wolves, which fight alone, against the gentle animals that flock together, and asks which we shall resemble. Hobbes answers that we are both: gods to one another inside a commonwealth, wolves between cities. Is the wolf in us a fault of character or a want of common institutions?

Milton turns the reading’s comparison upside down. In his poem even the fallen angels keep firm concord, and of all rational creatures only human beings disagree, though they live under hope of grace.

“He has endowed them with equal susceptibilities,” says the reading. Shylock argues the same from the body, organ by organ, to men who have spat on him, and in the lines that follow he claims an equal right to revenge.

The reading says that without its bonds the social body has no well-being or security. Donne, hearing a funeral bell from his sickbed, arrives at the same dependence from the other side: every death takes something from him.
A proverb shared in one form or another by many peoples of southern Africa says of the person what the reading says of the social body: it exists only through its relationships.

Against the reading’s social body Emerson speaks for the single member. A society can ask conformity as the price of its security, and he refuses to pay. What must a united community do to avoid becoming his joint-stock company?

The reading asks us to love all humankind as leaves of one tree. A doctor in Dostoevsky’s novel admits the difficulty: love for humanity can grow as love for the person in the room shrinks. The elder who tells the story prescribes active love, practised on particular people.

The reading says all existing things are connected and that the connection sustains life. Muir, a naturalist spending a summer in the Sierra Nevada, found the same whenever he tried to study one thing alone.
Six words state the reading’s claim about living beings: they exist by helping one another. In the Jain sūtra this is a description of how souls are, before it is advice.

The reading denies that creatures can live singly. Gibran, speaking of marriage, supplies the other half: those who are joined still need room between them. Does his counsel to two people hold for a family of peoples?

The reading pictures humankind as one tree with nations for branches. The Great Law plants a Tree of Peace whose roots run to the four directions, so that any nation willing to keep the peace may follow a root to its shelter.

Speaking in Athens, Paul agrees with the reading that all nations are of one blood. Then he says what the reading denies, that God fixed the bounds of their habitation, and gives the reason: so that each might seek him. Can a boundary serve a purpose without becoming a barrier?
The reading calls the surface of the earth one native land. The oldest recorded form of that claim is a philosopher’s reply to a question about his home town.

Two neighbours rebuild a wall every spring. One doubts it, one repeats his father’s saying, and the poem lets neither win. The reading calls national boundaries imaginary; Frost’s speaker asks the earlier question of any wall: what is it keeping in or out, and whom might it offend?

Written under foreign rule, the prayer asks for freedom and in the same breath for a world not broken up by “narrow domestic walls”: the reading’s imaginary barriers, seen from a country that wanted its independence.

Gandhi accepts the reading’s open world and adds a condition. He wants every culture to blow through his house, and he will not be blown off his feet by any of them. Is unity with others possible without a place of one’s own to stand?

The reading says humankind was created from one progeny in order to associate in fellowship. The verse gives the same purpose to difference itself: nations and tribes exist so that people may come to know one another, and honour lies in conduct.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá took a dinner shared by Persians and Americans as evidence of human unity. Half a century later King made the shared table the picture of a hope still unmet in his own country.
The poem sees the table from the place of the one sent to eat in the kitchen. Beside the reading it asks who was missing from the tables that proved unity, and who decides when everyone may sit down.

The reading says we were created for unity and harmony, not discord. Kant holds that nature uses discord: rivalry wakes capacities that would sleep in an easy concord. Can discord serve the purpose the reading names, or does it only delay it?

“Ye are even as a single soul,” the letter tells its readers. Whitman opens his poem with the same claim in the first person and rests it on shared matter: what is his is as good as yours, atom for atom.

Scripture’s oldest story of a single united people ends with God scattering them, because nothing would be beyond their reach. The reading promises that oneness will end strife. What separates the unity it hopes for from the unity of Babel?

Aristotle is answering Plato, who made unity the highest good of a city. Pressed far enough, he argues, unity destroys what it unites, because a community is by nature a plurality. The reading foresees native lands, races and religions made one; where would Aristotle have it stop?
Long before the reading, a young English poet gave its hope a political form: the war-drum silent and the nations met in one parliament.

The quatrain ends where the reading does, with East and West dissolved. For the reading they are positions on a sphere and nothing more. For Kipling they vanish only when two strong men stand face to face.

The reading rests human equality on God’s justice. The Declaration, written after a world war for peoples of every belief, asserts the same equality with no ground named but reason and conscience, and ends on the reading’s word, brotherhood.
Orwell’s pigs keep the commandment and add a clause. The line warns every community that proclaims equality: the words can stay on the wall after the practice has gone.
The reading calls cooperation and reciprocity the essential bonds. Asked for one word to live by, Confucius chose the same one and defined it by the rule most traditions share.

Smith begins where the reading does: no one can live without the help of multitudes. But he doubts that goodwill can supply it, and trusts each person’s interest instead. The reading speaks of an “economic conscience”. Which of the two holds a society together?

In the same years a Russian geographer argued the reading’s case from natural history, against those who read Darwin as a licence for unlimited competition: among animals, those that combine are the ones that thrive.
The Confucian classic climbs the reading’s ladder and adds a rung below the family. Order begins in the cultivated person and widens through family and state to the whole kingdom.

The reading widens the circle from family to continent. Burke insists that the first link must hold: love of the small group one belongs to is the germ of love for country and for mankind. Can a wider loyalty be learned without a nearer one?
“Weakness appeareth from discord and strength emergeth from unity.” The fable of the father and his bundle of sticks has taught that lesson to children for more than two thousand years.
The reading’s lamps differ in form and vessel and are one in their light. Rūmī uses the image to explain why religions disagree, which is where the guide’s next section goes.
The best-known verse on unity in the Hebrew Bible praises what the reading describes, a gathering that becomes unity of hearts.

“One Lord, one faith”: the letter gives the Christian form of the reading’s remedy, the union of all in one common Faith, and of the earlier reading that unity in its first degree is unity in religion.

Gandhi names the same sickness, the enmity of religious communities, and prescribes differently: not one religion but mutual respect among many. The reading’s remedy is one common Faith. Are these rival answers, or answers to different questions?

The verse says God could have made humankind one community and did not. Each has its law and its way, all are to compete in good works, and God will settle their differences. How does plurality by design sit beside the reading’s one common Faith?

The reading hopes the earth’s inhabitants will become citizens of one city. Plutarch reports that the founder of Stoicism made this the single principle of his ideal state, and adds that Zeno wrote it as a dream.

Paul’s sentence is the reading’s nearest ancestor: the labels of nation, rank and sex are named and set aside. He adds “in Christ Jesus”. The reading describes a gathering of people who have laid such prejudices down.
The reading asks the followers of religions to worship in one another’s places of worship. In a love poem by the Andalusian mystic, the heart has itself become every such place at once.

Cut into rock by a Buddhist emperor of India, the edict gives the reading’s counsel as public policy: praising one’s own religion at the expense of others harms it, so go and listen to what the others teach.
The tenth Sikh Guru says of temple and mosque what the reading asks worshippers to act upon, and rests it, like an earlier reading, on the body: the same eyes and ears, the same four elements.
The prayer “that they all may be one” is the charter of every movement for Christian unity. Its scope is those who will believe; the reading states the same desire for the entire human race.
The verse puts the reading’s argument in one sentence: all the wealth on earth could not have joined these hearts; God joined them.

The most famous call to unity of the modern age rests on the opposite premise. For Marx and Engels a shared material condition, not a spiritual power, will unite people across every border, and the unity is that of one class against another.
A clergyman’s dry sentence states the failure the reading condemns. Swift stops at the diagnosis; the reading draws the conclusion that a religion which causes enmity were better absent.
Pascal, a believer, goes further than the reading. Religious conviction does not merely fail to prevent harm; it can make harm complete and cheerful. What in a religion guards against this?

The Quaker founder of Pennsylvania applies the reading’s test of a true religion to persons. Those in whom religion has produced humility and mercy already belong together, and only their outward liveries keep them strangers.
The prophet’s three questions follow the reading’s own order: one Father, one Creator, and therefore, why do we wrong one another?

Some three thousand years before the reading, a Vedic hymn says that what is one is called by many names. The reading places the difference in the mirrors that receive one light; the hymn places it in the speech of the wise.

Shelley’s dome of many-coloured glass is the reading’s mirror in another material: one white light, stained by whatever receives it. He is mourning Keats, and for him only death restores the white radiance.

Closing the first Parliament of Religions, a Hindu monk set a limit to unity: each faith should take in the spirit of the others and still grow by its own law. The reading asks all to acknowledge every heaven-sent Teacher. Do the two ask the same thing?

The reading speaks of fevers in the world of the mind that only the teachings of God can abate. The founders of UNESCO agreed on the place, the minds of men, and chose another medicine: knowledge of each other’s ways and lives.
The Buddhist verse gives the rule the reading applies to nations: hatred is never ended by hatred. It calls this an old rule already.

The prophet shares the reading’s vision of nations at peace and ends it differently. Each man sits under his own vine, and each people walks in the name of its own god. Can the peace of the first verse be had together with the plurality of the last?
The reading says that whatever in religion caused hardship and strife has been set aside. The Qur’an’s shortest statement on the matter removes the first cause of religious strife, which is coercion.

The reading asks why parts of one tree should be at strife. The emperor follows the image through: a branch may be cut off by another hand, but a person cuts himself off, by hatred, from the whole tree of humankind.

An early Christian describes his community much as the reading describes another, seventeen centuries later: at home in every country, strangers in none, and known by the way they live among their neighbours.

The Confucian picture of the age of Grand Union is close to the reading’s: people care for more than their own parents and children, and doors stand open. The classic places that age in the past; the reading places it ahead.
The verse tells the reading’s history in the same order: humankind was one community, scripture came to settle its differences, and those who received it fell out over it.

A rabbi speaking at a Christian seminary gives leaders of religion the reason for the duty the reading lays on them. Borrowing Donne’s island, he says the faiths are already bound together, and that the failure of one harms all.
At the end of a civil war a president asks for what the reading calls its whole purpose: an end to rancour, and a peace that reaches beyond one nation to all.
Job applies the reading’s rule to the hardest case, his own servants. He may not despise their cause, because the one who made him made them.

The reading says the variety of forms and colours has a divine purpose. The verse counts the difference of human languages and colours among the signs of God, beside the creation of the heavens and the earth.
The rabbis find the Creator’s greatness in the very fact the reading defends. A human mint strikes coins that are all alike; every person bears the stamp of the first, and no two are the same.

A Daoist adds a warning to the reading’s praise of variety. To make the different alike, by lengthening the duck’s legs or shortening the crane’s, causes pain. What would it mean to unite people without doing that?
Du Bois had already named the question the reading calls regrettable as the problem of the twentieth century, and not of America alone.
A lone dissenting judge gave American law the reading’s own image, eyes closed to colour, on the day the Supreme Court approved segregation.

Eighty-two years after Harlan, another justice of the same court argued that the road to a society blind to colour runs first through seeing it. If the reading states the goal, does it also settle the means?

The play that gave America its best-known image of unity opened four years before ‘Abdu’l-Bahá spoke there, and its image is the reverse of his. In the crucible differences melt into one metal; in the garden each flower keeps its colour and lends charm to the rest.

Answering Zangwill three years after ‘Abdu’l-Bahá spoke of the garden, an American philosopher chose a kindred image: an orchestra in which each people keeps its own instrument and the music needs them all, discords included.

The most quoted sentence of the Atlanta address offered unity in work together with separation in social life. The reading asks for the first, “mutual advancement”, and other readings refuse the second. Can a hand be one if its fingers never touch?
Speaking to the United Nations, the emperor of Ethiopia made the reading’s link between the equality of races and the peace of the world, and stated it as a condition.

The reading declares women and men one and the same in the Kingdom of God. A convention of American women had claimed that equality for this world by adding two words to the Declaration of Independence.
The Sanskrit behind the reading’s “one great universal family” comes from this verse, which treats the sorting of people into mine and theirs as a small mind’s arithmetic.

The reading asks why Parliament is roused by twenty-five deaths and silent about six thousand. Smith described the mechanism: a man would lose more sleep over his little finger than over the ruin of a hundred million people he will never see. He goes on to ask what restrains us even so.

The verse supplies the arithmetic the reading asks for, in which one life already counts as all. It presents the rule as one first given to the Children of Israel, and the Mishnah states it a few lines before the passages quoted in this guide.

Almost word for word the reading’s ideal: to regard another’s state, family and person as one’s own. Mozi taught it in China in the fifth century before Christ and argued that it would end war, usurpation and theft.

The best-known objection to Mozi, from the next great Confucian. To love all equally, Mencius says, is to deny the particular affection owed to a father. The reading widens concern from family to humankind. Does it ask us to love all equally?
Written from a jail cell to clergymen who had called him an outsider, King’s sentences give the reading’s thought its modern form: harm done anywhere reaches everyone.
A peace-maker’s maxim from the religious wars of the seventeenth century draws the reading’s line between essential unity and lesser differences, and names the virtue that must cover both.
The reading expects knowledge to free people from prejudice. Twain, at the end of a long journey abroad, names the kind of knowledge he found to work: meeting other people where they live.
After twenty-seven years in prison, Mandela gives the reason the reading’s hope is not naive: prejudice is learned, and what is learned can be taught otherwise.
‘Abdu’l-Bahá wishes two inherited names away so that one may remain. Juliet has seen what an inherited name can do: it is the name, not the person, that is her enemy.

The reading hopes two designations will give way to one. Du Bois describes a person who carries two names at once and asks to keep both, without either being used against him. When does a single name unite, and when does it erase?
Paul meets the same habit in Corinth, where believers name themselves after their teachers, and answers as the reading does: the names divide what is one.

leftOut.saying: “If you want to go fast, go alone; if you want to go far, go together.”
leftOut.reason: No source for it as the proverb of any people was established in this pilot, so it was left out. The Zulu proverb on personhood stands in its place.

leftOut.saying: “Be the change you wish to see in the world.”
leftOut.reason: Left out unverified: no place in his writings was found for it. Two passages from Young India, with their dates, are used instead.

leftOut.saying: “Man did not weave the web of life; he is merely a strand in it.”
leftOut.reason: Left out: the attribution is doubtful and no primary text was reached. The Great Law of Peace stands as the voice from Indigenous North America.

leftOut.saying: The songs “Imagine”, “One Love” and “We Are the World”.
leftOut.attributed: John Lennon; Bob Marley; Michael Jackson and Lionel Richie.
leftOut.reason: Among the best-known statements of the theme, and omitted: song lyrics are licensed more strictly than other texts, and no line of a lyric is quoted in this pilot.

leftOut.attributed: Sigmund Freud, Civilization and Its Discontents.
leftOut.reason: Wanted beside the reading on minor differences. No openly readable text of a named translation was found to check the wording against.

leftOut.saying: Sayings of Black Elk, T. H. White and the astronaut Sultan bin Salman Al Saud.
leftOut.attributed: Black Elk Speaks; The Once and Future King; The Home Planet.
leftOut.reason: Each was a candidate; none could be checked against a readable text of its source in the time given, and each book is still in copyright.
